<reason>Both sides argued tightly and answered pressure questions cleanly with proper A1/A2 formatting, but A found and pressed a genuine internal tension in B's case that B never resolved. B's justification for the mandate rests on bot-driven theft at scarce, high-demand events; but when pressed on scope, B conceded leakage precisely at "the highest-demand games" and retreated to "most tickets" meaning the ordinary Tuesday show — exactly the tickets where bot extraction was never the real problem. A explicitly exploited this in Rebuttal 2 and Closing ("the mandate clears the most verified marketplace of precisely the tickets most needing verification"), and B's rejoinder ("CON needs the Tuesday show to also break") never actually closed the gap between the policy's stated rationale and its admitted failure zone. B's platform self-dealing point remained live and rhetorically strong ("guaranteed harm vs. contingent harm"), and A somewhat dropped explicit engagement with it in the closing, but A's earlier point that self-dealing is better solved by structural separation than a blanket price mandate blunted its force as a reason this specific remedy is necessary. On balance, A's efficacy critique landed harder and went less answered than B's justice-framed critique, giving A the cleaner path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2/Closing point that B's own concession of leakage at "the highest-demand games" undercuts the policy exactly where the bot-extraction problem B relies on actually occurs, versus B's unresolved "that's just an outlier" reply.</best_rebuttal>
